title: AVL Trees & Self-Balancing
summary: An AVL tree is a self-balancing BST that keeps the height difference between left and right subtrees at most 1 at every node. Rotations restore balance and guarantee O(log n) operations.

blocks.content: Each node in an AVL tree tracks its balance factor (BF) = height(left subtree) − height(right subtree).
BF of -1, 0, or +1 means the node is balanced. When BF reaches ±2, rotations restore balance.

items: BF of all ancestors must be updated after insertion/deletion
Height of an n-node AVL tree: O(log n) guaranteed

blocks.alt: AVL tree LL and RR rotations

blocks.content: LL case: insertion into the left subtree of the left child → resolved with a right rotation.
RR case: insertion into the right subtree of the right child → resolved with a left rotation. Rotations are O(1) and preserve the BST invariant.

items: Right rotation: left child becomes new root, old root becomes right child
Left rotation: right child becomes new root, old root becomes left child
Must verify BST property (left < root < right) holds after rotation

blocks.content: LR case: insertion into the right subtree of the left child → left-rotate the left child, then right-rotate the root.
RL case: insertion into the left subtree of the right child → right-rotate the right child, then left-rotate the root.

items: LR = Left Rotate(left child) + Right Rotate(root)
RL = Right Rotate(right child) + Left Rotate(root)
Four cases in total: LL, RR, LR, RL
At most one rotation (single or double) needed to rebalance after insertion

blocks.content: AVL trees maintain strict balance (height diff ≤ 1), making lookups faster, but require more rotations on insertion/deletion.
Red-Black trees allow looser balance (height diff ≤ 2 log n), making updates faster. Production libraries (Java TreeMap, C++ std::map) typically choose Red-Black.

items: AVL: faster lookups, more rotations on updates
Red-Black: faster updates, slightly slower lookups
